title: The Second World War
description: The war of 1939 to 1945 across the world, from Japan’s war in China and the Munich crisis through Dunkirk, Barbarossa, Pearl Harbor, Stalingrad, the Holocaust, the Bengal famine, Imphal and D-Day to Berlin, Hiroshima and the United Nations.
note: Midway is given at longitude 182.6 (177.4°W) so it sits on this map’s eastern edge. Powers areas are loose regions, not borders, and the front lines are simplified.

steps.title: War in China
steps.text: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and set up a puppet state, Manchukuo. In July 1937 a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing became full war with China. Japanese troops took Shanghai and then Nanjing, the Nationalist capital, where they killed civilians and prisoners for weeks. Death estimates are disputed, from tens of thousands to over 300,000.
steps.today: The Memorial Hall of the Nanjing Massacre stands on a site of mass killings in the city.

steps.title: Munich
steps.text: Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party took power in Germany in 1933, crushed opponents, persecuted Jews and rearmed. Germany absorbed Austria in March 1938. At Munich that September, Britain and France agreed to let Hitler take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia, hoping to keep the peace. Britain’s Neville Chamberlain called it peace for our time. In March 1939 Germany seized Prague.
steps.today: The building where the agreement was signed is now Munich’s university of music and theatre.

steps.title: The invasion of Poland
steps.text: In August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact that secretly divided eastern Europe between them. On 1 September German forces invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war two days later. On 17 September the Soviet army invaded from the east. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September. Both occupiers arrested and killed Poland’s officers, priests and teachers.
steps.today: Warsaw’s Old Town, destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt from paintings and plans, is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The fall of France
steps.text: In April 1940 Germany took Denmark and Norway. On 10 May it attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France, with tanks pushing through the Ardennes forest to the Channel. Some 338,000 trapped British and French troops were taken off the beaches at Dunkirk, many by small civilian boats. Paris fell on 14 June, and France signed an armistice on 22 June.
steps.today: Dunkirk is a port in northern France; a museum there tells the story of the evacuation.

steps.title: The Battle of Britain
steps.text: Britain, now led by Winston Churchill, fought on alone in Europe, backed by its empire. Through the summer of 1940 the Royal Air Force, with Polish, Czech and other pilots, beat off the German air force, and invasion was put off. The bombing of London and other cities, the Blitz, went on until May 1941 and killed some 43,000 civilians.
steps.today: The Churchill War Rooms, the bunker under Whitehall, are now a museum.

steps.title: Operation Barbarossa
steps.text: On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million men. They took Kyiv, began a siege of Leningrad that lasted almost 900 days, and reached the edge of Moscow. In December a Soviet counter-attack in deep winter drove them back. Behind the German armies, killing squads shot Jews by the hundred thousand.
steps.today: Moscow is the capital of Russia; Victory Day, 9 May, is the country’s biggest public holiday.

steps.title: Pearl Harbor
steps.text: Japan, short of oil after American sanctions, decided to seize the resources of South-East Asia. On 7 December 1941 its carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, sinking or damaging eight battleships and killing about 2,400 Americans. The United States declared war on Japan; Germany and Italy then declared war on the United States.
steps.today: The USS Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor stands over the sunken battleship, which still holds most of its dead crew.

steps.title: The fall of Singapore
steps.text: Within months Japan took Hong Kong, the Philippines, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies and Burma. Singapore, Britain’s great naval base, surrendered on 15 February 1942, and some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops were captured. Many Indian prisoners joined the Indian National Army, which from 1943, under Subhas Chandra Bose, fought alongside Japan against British rule in India.
steps.today: Kranji War Memorial in Singapore holds the graves of Allied soldiers who died in the region.

steps.title: Midway
steps.text: American code-breakers had read enough of Japan’s naval signals to learn of its plan to take Midway atoll. On 4 June 1942 US carrier planes sank four of the Japanese carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor, for the loss of one American carrier. Japan never replaced the lost ships and trained pilots, and the Pacific war turned towards the Allies.
steps.today: Midway Atoll is a US wildlife refuge, home to huge colonies of albatrosses, with a memorial to the battle.

steps.title: El Alamein
steps.text: In North Africa, Italian and then German forces under Erwin Rommel fought the British Eighth Army back and forth across Libya and into Egypt. At El Alamein, west of Alexandria, Bernard Montgomery’s army, with Indian, Australian, New Zealand and South African divisions, broke through in November 1942. Days later American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria.
steps.today: Commonwealth, German and Italian war cemeteries stand near El Alamein on Egypt’s coast.

steps.title: Stalingrad
steps.text: In 1942 the German army drove south towards the oilfields of the Caucasus and reached Stalingrad on the Volga. The city was fought over street by street. In November Soviet armies encircled the German Sixth Army, and its commander, Friedrich Paulus, surrendered on 2 February 1943. Deaths on both sides are disputed estimates, around a million or more.
steps.today: The city, now Volgograd, is crowned by the statue The Motherland Calls on the Mamayev Kurgan.

steps.title: The Holocaust
steps.text: Nazi Germany set out to murder all of Europe’s Jews. Killing squads shot Jews across the occupied Soviet lands from 1941, and death camps were built in occupied Poland. At Auschwitz-Birkenau alone about 1.1 million people were killed, most of them Jews. In all about six million Jews were murdered, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners and many others.
steps.today: Auschwitz-Birkenau is a museum and memorial; 27 January, the day it was liberated in 1945, is Holocaust Memorial Day.

steps.title: The Bengal famine
steps.text: In 1943 famine struck Bengal. The loss of rice from Japanese-held Burma, a cyclone, wartime inflation, hoarding and a slow and inadequate response by the colonial government all played a part, and so did decisions in London on food exports and shipping. Historians still argue over how much weight each deserves. Deaths are estimated at about 2 to 3 million.
steps.today: Kolkata, then Calcutta, is the capital of West Bengal.

steps.title: Imphal and Kohima
steps.text: In March 1944 Japan invaded India from Burma, with Indian National Army units alongside. At Imphal and Kohima, the British Fourteenth Army, mostly Indian soldiers from a volunteer army that grew to about 2.5 million, held on through weeks of siege. Japan lost tens of thousands of men, many to starvation and disease, and in 1945 the Allies retook Burma.
steps.today: Kohima’s war cemetery bears the words: When you go home, tell them of us and say, for your tomorrow, we gave our today.

steps.title: D-Day
steps.text: On 6 June 1944 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on five beaches in Normandy: the largest seaborne invasion in history. They broke out in August, Paris was liberated on 25 August, and by autumn the Allies had reached Germany’s border. In the east that summer, a Soviet offensive destroyed a German army group.
steps.today: The beaches keep their code names, such as Omaha and Juno; the American cemetery above Omaha holds over 9,000 graves.

steps.title: The fall of Berlin
steps.text: Soviet armies crossed Poland in January 1945, and the camps were liberated as the Allies advanced. American and Soviet troops met on the Elbe on 25 April while the Red Army fought its way into Berlin. Hitler killed himself on 30 April. Germany surrendered unconditionally, and 8 May became Victory in Europe Day; Russia marks it on 9 May.
steps.today: The Reichstag, where Soviet soldiers raised their flag in 1945, again houses Germany’s parliament.

steps.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
steps.native: 広島・長崎への原爆投下
steps.text: After Iwo Jima, Okinawa and the firebombing of Tokyo, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August. By the end of 1945 they had killed an estimated 150,000 to 250,000 people. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August, and Japan announced its surrender on 15 August.
steps.today: The ruined dome nearest the blast, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The United Nations
steps.text: Fifty nations signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco in June 1945. The war had killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, most of them civilians. Axis leaders were tried at Nuremberg and Tokyo. Europe was soon split between the United States and the Soviet Union, and within a few years India and much of Asia were free.
steps.today: The UN is based in New York; the charter was signed in San Francisco’s War Memorial Veterans Building.

items.name: Adolf Hitler
items.text: Born in Austria, he served in the German army in the First World War and led the Nazi party to power in 1933. As dictator he rearmed Germany, began the war in Europe by invading Poland and ordered the murder of Europe’s Jews. He killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945 as Soviet troops closed in.

items.name: Winston Churchill
items.text: British prime minister from May 1940, as France was falling. His speeches rallied Britain to fight on, and he built the alliance with the United States and, from 1941, the Soviet Union. He was voted out in July 1945. His record on India, including his government’s handling of the Bengal famine, is sharply criticised.

items.name: Joseph Stalin
items.text: Ruler of the Soviet Union from the late 1920s. His purges had killed much of the army’s officer corps before the war, and in 1939 he made a pact with Hitler and took eastern Poland. After Germany invaded, he led the Soviet war effort at enormous cost in lives, and after victory imposed communist rule on eastern Europe.

items.name: Georgy Zhukov
items.text: A Soviet general who organised the defence of Leningrad and Moscow in 1941 and helped plan the encirclement at Stalingrad. He commanded the final assault on Berlin in 1945 and accepted Germany’s surrender there. Stalin later sidelined him, but he returned as defence minister after Stalin’s death.

items.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
items.text: President of the United States from 1933 until his death in April 1945. Before Pearl Harbor he sent Britain weapons on credit through Lend-Lease; afterwards he led the country through the war. He planned the United Nations with Churchill and Stalin, but died weeks before Germany’s surrender and the San Francisco conference.

items.name: Hideki Tojo
items.text: A general who was prime minister of Japan from October 1941 to July 1944 and led the government that chose war with the United States. He resigned after the loss of Saipan. Tried by the Allies in Tokyo, he was hanged in 1948 as a war criminal.

items.name: Subhas Chandra Bose
items.role: Leader of the Indian National Army
items.text: A leader of the Indian National Congress who broke with Gandhi over the use of force. He escaped British house arrest in 1941 and sought help from Germany, then Japan. From 1943 he led the Indian National Army and a provisional government. He is reported to have died after a plane crash in Taiwan in 1945, which some still dispute.

items.name: Anne Frank
items.text: A Jewish girl born in Frankfurt whose family fled to Amsterdam. From 1942 they hid in rooms behind her father’s business, where she kept a diary. They were betrayed in 1944, and Anne died in Bergen-Belsen in early 1945, aged 15. Her diary, published by her father, the family’s only survivor, is among the world’s most read books.
